gloss_terse: burden-bearer, laborer who carries heavy loads for construction or transport
gloss_readable: A late Hebrew noun designating one who carries heavy burdens, used collectively for laborers conscripted for building projects. Solomon employed tens of thousands of these workers alongside stonecutters for the Temple (1 Kgs 5:15; 2 Chr 2:2, 18), and Josiah similarly organized them for Temple repairs (2 Chr 34:13). In Nehemiah 4:10, the burden-bearers' flagging strength becomes a metaphor for the people's discouragement during wall reconstruction. The English 'burden-bearers' and Spanish 'cargadores' both capture the collective labor force sense.

senses.1: Burden-bearer or carrier employed in large-scale construction, used collectively for conscripted labor gangs. Solomon's Temple workforce included 70,000 of these alongside 80,000 stonecutters (2 Chr 2:2). The English 'burden-bearers,' Spanish 'los-cargadores,' and French 'porteur' all converge on the notion of heavy manual labor. In Nehemiah 4:10, their weakening strength signals the demoralization of the rebuilding effort.

gloss_terse: prefect, provincial governor or high-ranking administrative official in the Babylonian/Persian empire
gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun denoting a high-ranking provincial official in the Babylonian-Persian administrative hierarchy. All five occurrences appear in Daniel, where prefects are listed alongside satraps, counselors, and judges in formal enumerations of imperial officials (Dan 3:2-3, 27). Daniel himself is elevated above these prefects after interpreting Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Dan 2:48), and Darius's officials conspire among them (Dan 6:7). The term is an Assyrian loanword reflecting Mesopotamian bureaucratic structure.

senses.1: A high-ranking administrative officer in the Babylonian-Persian governmental hierarchy, consistently listed among other imperial officials in formal court enumerations. English 'prefects,' Spanish 'los-prefectos,' French 'préfet,' and German 'Beamte' (officials) all point to the bureaucratic rank. Daniel is elevated above these officials (Dan 2:48), and they appear as a class in Nebuchadnezzar's assembly (Dan 3:2-3) and Darius's court (Dan 6:7).

gloss_terse: end, conclusion, final point of a matter, place, or process
gloss_readable: A late Hebrew synonym for the more common qets, denoting the terminal point of something whether spatial, temporal, or conceptual. It marks the end of a wadi where Jehoshaphat's army found plunder (2 Chr 20:16), the rear of a locust swarm driven into the sea (Joel 2:20), and the incomprehensible scope of God's work from beginning to end (Eccl 3:11). In Ecclesiastes 12:13, it serves as the grand summation: the conclusion of the whole matter. The breadth of the Spanish glosses—'al-final-de,' 'el-fin,' 'fin-de'—mirrors this versatility.

senses.1: The terminal point, conclusion, or final extent of something—whether a physical location (end of a wadi, 2 Chr 20:16), a natural phenomenon (rear of a locust swarm, Joel 2:20), or an abstract matter (conclusion of all instruction, Eccl 12:13). English 'end,' Spanish 'fin/el-fin,' French 'fin,' and German 'Ende' uniformly reflect termination. Ecclesiastes 3:11 uses it theologically: God's work stretches from beginning to 'soph,' beyond human comprehension.

gloss_terse: end, conclusion, extremity (Aramaic); the final point of a matter, place, or duration
gloss_readable: The Aramaic cognate of Hebrew soph, used exclusively in Daniel to denote an end or extremity. It describes the reach of a great tree extending to the end of the earth in Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Dan 4:11, 22), the everlasting nature of God's dominion (Dan 6:26, 'to the end'), the destruction of dominion at the appointed end (Dan 7:26), and the conclusion of Daniel's vision account (Dan 7:28). The consistent Spanish rendering 'fin/el-fin' and English 'end' confirm a single cohesive meaning across all contexts.

senses.1: The terminal point or conclusion of something in Aramaic usage, spanning spatial extent (a tree reaching to the end of the earth, Dan 4:11, 22), temporal duration ('to the end' meaning forever, Dan 6:26; or an appointed termination, Dan 7:26), and narrative closure (end of the matter, Dan 7:28). English 'end/the-end,' Spanish 'fin/el-fin/hasta-el-fin-de,' and French 'fin' all converge on this single sense of finality.

gloss_terse: to drag, haul away by force; drag corpses, captives, or objects along the ground
gloss_readable: A verb conveying the forceful dragging of something or someone, always with connotations of violence or compulsion. Hushai proposes dragging an entire city with ropes into a ravine (2 Sam 17:13), while Jeremiah prophesies corpses dragged through Jerusalem's gates (Jer 15:3; 22:19) and captives hauled away like sheep seized by a predator (Jer 49:20 = 50:45). The Spanish 'arrastrar' (to drag along the ground) and the English 'drag' both preserve the visceral physicality of the action.

senses.1: To drag or haul forcibly, typically involving violence, humiliation, or brute compulsion. Hushai envisions dragging a whole city into a valley with ropes (2 Sam 17:13); Jeremiah describes corpses dragged ignominiously (Jer 15:3; 22:19) and captives hauled off like sheep by a predator (Jer 49:20 = 50:45). Spanish 'arrastrando/para-arrastrar' and English 'drag/dragged' consistently capture the forceful, ground-level movement. The Moabite Stone cognate confirms the same concrete sense.

gloss_terse: thorn, brier; also hook (for fishing or dragging)
gloss_readable: A noun with two distinct but related senses rooted in the idea of something sharp and piercing. As 'thorns,' it appears in images of desolation (Isa 34:13), as a barrier God sets in the path of the unfaithful (Hos 2:6), and in Qoheleth's vivid simile of thorns crackling uselessly under a pot (Eccl 7:6). As 'hooks,' it describes the instruments by which Amos warns Samaria's women will be dragged away (Amos 4:2). The French split between 'épines' (thorns) and 'pots' reflects the interpretive complexity of Ecclesiastes 7:6, where both thorns and a cooking pot appear together.

senses.1: Sharp thorny plants signifying desolation, obstruction, or futility. Thorns overgrow Edom's palaces as a sign of divine judgment (Isa 34:13), God hedges an unfaithful wife's path with thorns (Hos 2:6), and the crackling of thorns under a pot illustrates the fool's hollow laughter (Eccl 7:6). Spanish 'espinos' and French 'épines' both point to brier-plants. Nahum 1:10 likely references entanglement among thorns, though the text is difficult. The related sense of 'hooks' (Amos 4:2, Spanish 'anzuelos') derives from the same sharp-pointed semantic root, used for fishhooks or dragging-hooks by which captives are led away.

gloss_terse: to come up, ascend, arise (Aramaic); of physical or figurative rising
gloss_readable: An Aramaic verb meaning to come up or ascend, appearing exclusively in Daniel and Ezra. It describes the four great beasts rising from the sea in Daniel's vision (Dan 7:3), the little horn coming up among the ten (Dan 7:8, 20), and thoughts arising in Nebuchadnezzar's mind on his bed (Dan 2:29). In Ezra 4:12, it reports that Jews have 'come up' from exile to Jerusalem. The Spanish renderings—'subiendo,' 'subieron,' 'subió'—consistently reflect upward movement, whether literal or figurative.

senses.1: To come up, ascend, or arise, used of both physical and visionary movement in Aramaic contexts. Beasts ascend from the sea (Dan 7:3), a horn comes up among others (Dan 7:8, 20), exiles come up to Jerusalem (Ezra 4:12), and thoughts arise in the mind (Dan 2:29). Spanish 'subir' (subiendo/subieron/subió) uniformly captures the upward directionality. The Haph'el causative form means 'to lift up' or 'bring up' (Dan 3:22; 6:24), extending the same spatial logic.

gloss_terse: image, idol figure, statue set up for worship or veneration
gloss_readable: A noun denoting a carved or sculpted image, possibly originating as the name of a foreign deity before becoming a generic term for idol-statues. In Deuteronomy 4:16, Moses warns against making a 'pesel temunat kol-semel'—a carved image in the form of any figure—linking it to the broader prohibition against idolatry. Manasseh places such an idol in the Temple itself (2 Chr 33:7), later removing it in repentance (2 Chr 33:15). Ezekiel encounters the provocative 'image of jealousy' at the Temple's north gate (Ezek 8:3, 5), an idol so offensive it arouses God's jealous anger. The Phoenician cognate confirms its use as a standard term for cult images.

senses.1: An idol-image or cultic statue, a physical representation set up for worship that provokes divine jealousy. Deuteronomy 4:16 prohibits making any such figure; Manasseh installs one in the Temple (2 Chr 33:7) and later removes it (2 Chr 33:15). Ezekiel 8:3, 5 describes the 'semel of jealousy' at the Temple gate. English 'image/idol,' Spanish 'ídolo/imagen,' and French 'image/figure' all converge on the sense of a physical cult object. The Phoenician cognate semel/semelet confirms widespread Northwest Semitic usage for divine representations.

gloss_terse: fin (of a fish); a distinguishing mark of ritually clean aquatic creatures
gloss_readable: A technical term from the Levitical dietary laws designating the fin of a fish or aquatic creature. It appears exclusively in the parallel legal texts of Leviticus 11:9-12 and Deuteronomy 14:9-10, always paired with scales (qasqeseth) as the two markers that determine whether a water-dwelling creature is clean and permissible to eat. Creatures with both fins and scales are clean; those lacking either are 'an abomination.' The remarkable consistency across languages—English 'fin,' Spanish 'aleta,' French 'nageoire,' German 'fin'—reflects the precision of this biological-legal category.

senses.1: The fin of an aquatic creature, functioning as one of two required markers (alongside scales) for ritual cleanness in the dietary laws. All five occurrences appear in Leviticus 11:9-12 and Deuteronomy 14:9-10, where the presence of both fins and scales determines edibility. English 'fin,' Spanish 'aleta,' French 'nageoire,' and German 'fin' all point to the same anatomical feature. The term carries no metaphorical extension—it is purely a taxonomic criterion within Israel's holiness code.

gloss_terse: to join, attach oneself to; to be gathered together or associated with a group
gloss_readable: A verb expressing the idea of joining or attaching oneself to another person or group, spanning voluntary association, desperate petition, and involuntary clinging. A destitute priest's descendant begs to be attached to any priestly office for survival (1 Sam 2:36), while David laments being driven from attaching himself to the Lord's inheritance (1 Sam 26:19). Prophetically, nations will attach themselves to the house of Jacob (Isa 14:1). The Spanish range—'agrégame' (attach me), 'de-unirme' (from joining myself), 'se-juntan' (they gather)—captures the spectrum from individual plea to collective association.

senses.1: To join, attach, or associate oneself with a person, group, or inheritance, covering a range from desperate personal petition to national-scale incorporation. A ruined priestly family begs attachment to any office (1 Sam 2:36, Qal imperative); David grieves exclusion from the Lord's heritage (1 Sam 26:19, Hithpael); foreigners attach themselves to Israel (Isa 14:1, Niphal). Job 30:7 describes outcasts huddling together (Pual). Spanish 'agrégame/de-unirme/se-juntan' and French 'attach-moi' reflect the relational joining. Habakkuk 2:15 is textually uncertain but may involve 'joining' wrath to a cup.
